Messages.Author: berni...@attbi.comholdlespam
Messages.Body:
As I'm sure everyone may know (at least those who've actually read the
rulebook), Retainers that take damage in combat which are not killed are
immediately healed back to full post-combat.

However, if a Retainer is the target of a Cryptic Mission or Shadow Twin
outside of combat they lose that life permanently.

Isn't this a bit inconsistent? I'm not certain what the original game
designers had in mind, but seeing as the functionality of Allies is
being looked into by the RulesTeam maybe it's time that Retainers also
garnered a second look.

Why should it be so much harder to kill off a Retainer in comparison to
an Ally? Why shouldn't the "loss of life/blood"definition be consistent
across the board?

Anyone want to tackle this? Anyone agree or disagree?

BernieTime

As for the "if it ain't broke, don't fix it", with that philosophy you

Messages.Author: Halcyan 2
Messages.Body:
>It's not an earth-shattering topic that I'm raising here. I feel that
>how damage is dealt/received by allies, should be looked at in terms of
>consistency with regard to the rest of the game.

I agree that retainers are notoriously hard to kill. People in my playgroup do
on occasion decide to hurt retainers (though they usually find it more
worthwhile to hurt the opposing vampire).

In the case of smaller retainers like Raven Spies, Jackie, and Mr. Winthrop,
it's not that big of a problem. A single Theft or Thrown Gate takes them out.
Or just one Weather Control.

But once you start to hit 3 life (Wolf Companion) or the monstrous Stone Dog
(Gargoyles are cool!) Ghoul Escorts would be hard to kill too if they were
worth it.

So yes, making combat damage permanent to retainers would make the
heavy-hitters (3-4 life retainers) much easier to kill. But then again, how
about the case of 1-life "immune to non-agg" retainers. Aren't those guys even
*harder* to kill? And changing combat damage for retainers doesn't make *them*
any easier. (How rare is it for ranged aggravated damage to be directed at a
retainer?).

So overall, I'd go with the "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" philosophy.
Superficially, changing the rule might seem to depower some retainers. But it
would only be effective in a few cases and not in several others. Thus I doubt
it would really achieve the objective it has.

Halcyan 2

Messages.Author: LSJ
Messages.Body:
CurtAdams wrote:
>
> I always thought retainers auto-healed for a basic practical
> reason; if they had life counters it would be easy to mix them
> up with each other and with their employers. Never stated,
> but very obvious.

That's exactly right - the original design didn't have them using
life counters - they just had life as stated on the card. And, in
order to avoid having to keep track of the life, the rules writers
just had them heal up in short order.

But they didn't consider damage done outside of combat being tracked
over longer periods.

The current rules, however, recognize that retainer life has to be
tracked over long periods (possibly "for the rest of the game"),
and so retainers *do* have life counters. [6.1.4]

--

Halcyan 2 wrote:

> So overall, I'd go with the "if it ain't broke, don't fix it" philosophy.
> Superficially, changing the rule might seem to depower some retainers. But it
> would only be effective in a few cases and not in several others. Thus I doubt

Besides which, I'm somewhat confused why we were trying to "depower" any
retainers. Are there retainers that are overpowered? I'm sorry, but I haven't
noticed that the "Wolf Companion tactic" was responsible for any killer decks.

Bernie raised the issue of consistency, which is somewhat arguable, I guess.
Actually, I don't see consistency being that bad, per se, though I agree having
just a couple of effects that permanently wound retainers where everything else
only works on them if it can be done in a single combat doesn't strike me as very
lifelike or real. I have a bit more of an issue with these small-time exceptions
being difficult to remember (which may be Bernie's point, I don't know) and
therefore subject to being played inaccurately a lot more often than a rule which
is applied more regularly. But I'm not really sure it's _that_ broke, either.

Fred

Messages.Author: CurtAdams
Messages.Body:
vte...@white-wolf.com writes:

>>Counters on a retainer card are way too close.

>We use distinct counters for retainer's life (and for corruption
>counters, disease counters, etc. - anything that might get confused
>for the vampire's blood).

Of course there are ways around it. You need separate counters
for each retainer on a particular minion, though. The point of the
original (rather silly, actually) autoheal rule was to make the
game physically simpler and easier to play. IIRC, reducing Magic's
counter proliferation was an explicit goal. I respect that goal.
If you have to keep track of retainer life anyway, the autoheal
rule is just silly without a game benefit.

The point isn't about "de-powering" retainers, it's about consistency.
This is a very small aspect of the game, that if changed wouldn't have
sweeping changes to the game. True. But makes more sense
in relation to the rest of the game dynamic.

Vampires lose life
Allies lose life
Retainers are happy refill-em' up toadies

Why should retainers be any better than those that they serve?
It would be a small change that I cannot perceive to be objectionable,
though exploration of any possible ramifications is always a good idea.

Don't know if the RulesTeam would really look at this as there's no
huge player outcry for changing retainers. I brought it up as something
that should probably be looked into, so as to be consistent with the
rest of the game dynamics.

Sorry if the above isn't terribly clear, but I'm in a bit of a rush
today.
